summary: Points out the problem of delivering ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages to the intended server in ECMP load-balanced or anycast networks, where they can end up at the wrong machine. It discusses operational mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: A note saying 'your package is too big' goes to the wrong person and never reaches the sender. This explains how to fix that.

questions: why do icmpv6 packet too big messages get lost
how does ecmp affect path mtu discovery
why do icmp error messages get lost in load-balanced networks
how can routers detect packet too big messages
subtitle: When load balancers drop error messages about packet size

tldr.problem: When load-balanced networks use ECMP to spread traffic across multiple servers, ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages meant for one server often get routed to a different server, causing applications to fail silently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how intermediate routers compute which server receives an error message independently of the flow it relates to, and explains practical workarounds using filtering, policy routing, and broadcast proxying.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now deploy load balancing more reliably by detecting misrouted errors and broadcasting them to all servers, or by improving router handling of ICMP error payloads.

today: RFC 7690 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It documents an operational problem with ECMP load-balanced networks and provides practical mitigation techniques that network operators can deploy today.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large internet services use equal-cost multipath (ECMP) routing to split incoming connections across multiple servers or load balancers without keeping track of which server gets which connection. This spreads the load but creates a problem with error messages. When the network detects that a packet is too large to send—a situation called path MTU discovery—it sends an ICMPv6 type 2 message back to the sender. But because this error message looks nothing like the original flow, ECMP routing sends it to a random server instead of the one that needs the information.
sections.plainLanguage: A big company routes mail delivery to many workers by lottery. A returned 'package too big' notice gets randomly assigned to a worker who never sent the package, so it never reaches the right person.

sections.title: Why Packet Too Big Messages Get Lost
sections.content:
ECMP routers make forwarding decisions by computing a hash of the packet headers—typically the source and destination addresses, port numbers, and protocol. For data packets, this hash is consistent: all packets in the same flow hash to the same next hop. An ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message, however, contains the original packet as its payload but uses different addresses: it comes from the router that detected the problem, not from the server. The payload headers are not used in the hash calculation. Result: the error message hashes to a different server, one that has never seen the original flow.

This matters most when the limited MTU is caused by a tunnel on the path, which the client does not know about. Clients using technologies like Happy Eyeballs may actually prefer IPv4 and work around the problem, but operators expect path MTU discovery to work without manual tuning.
sections.plainLanguage: The error message is addressed to someone else, so the lottery routes it elsewhere. It's like a return notice with the wrong name on it.

sections.title: Practical Workarounds
sections.content:
The RFC describes two main approaches. One is to equip routers with the ability to look inside the ICMP payload and extract the original flow headers, then hash based on the reverse direction of the embedded flow. This requires capable hardware but produces the right result.

The second, more practical approach is to broadcast the error message to all servers under the assumption that the correct server will recognize the flow and update its route cache, while servers that do not recognize the flow will discard the message. Experience shows that the number of such messages in real deployments is small—perhaps 10 packets per second on a gigabit link of HTTPS traffic. A rate limiter can protect the servers from denial of service while allowing legitimate error messages through.

The RFC includes a Python script example using scapy that intercepts ICMPv6 type 2 messages and rebroadcasts them on Ethernet broadcast. Linux iptables can also be configured to duplicate the messages using the TEE target with appropriate rate limiting.
sections.plainLanguage: Option one: teach the router to look inside the error message and send it the right way. Option two: send it to everyone and let them ignore it if it is not theirs—like a town crier announcing the message in the town square.

sections.title: Better Solutions
sections.content: The RFC identifies three longer-term improvements. Routers could parse through the ICMP payload and re-hash based on the inner headers, effectively reversing the direction of the original flow. Networks could use policy routing or multicast trees to send ICMP errors to all the relevant servers. Most promising: widespread adoption of RFC 4821 (Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery) would reduce reliance on in-band ICMP error messages altogether, letting applications discover MTU limits through trial and observation instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Make routers smarter, use fancy routing tricks, or let applications figure out the size limit themselves without waiting for error messages.
